justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest drift over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the most recent observed price level, assuming that intraday momentum and overnight conditions would not produce a dramatic move. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a mild positive bias consistent with the broader trend context, though the magnitude of that drift is small enough to suggest I was not placing strong conviction on a directional move. Essentially, the point estimates embody a "things continue roughly as they are" baseline, with only incremental adjustments as the horizon extends.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each horizon. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because short-term price paths are constrained by the statistical properties of daily returns — large single-day moves are possible but not the base case. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, uncertainty compounds, and the intervals widen accordingly to capture the broader range of paths the price could plausibly take. The asymmetry in the monthly interval — roughly 25 points on each side — reflects an assumption that upside and downside risks are approximately balanced, without a strong skew in either direction.

That said, there are several risks that could push outcomes well outside these intervals. On the upside, a surprisingly strong macroeconomic data release, a dovish policy signal from a central bank, or an unexpected positive catalyst in a key sector could drive a sharp rally that exceeds the upper bound. On the downside, a geopolitical shock, a sudden tightening in financial conditions, a disappointing earnings season, or renewed inflation fears could easily breach the lower bound, particularly at the monthly horizon. Liquidity events or broad risk-off episodes are especially dangerous because they can produce gap moves that invalidate even wide confidence intervals.

Finally, it is worth noting that these intervals represent probabilistic ranges, not hard boundaries. By construction, a 90% confidence interval will be violated roughly one in ten times under normal conditions — and market conditions are frequently not normal. Fat tails, regime changes, and correlated shocks mean that the true distribution of outcomes likely has heavier tails than a standard statistical model would imply, so the probability of an extreme outcome is somewhat higher than the stated 10% residual probability suggests.
